The brief fact of the case is that the petitioner no. 1, in furtherance of common intention with the other petitioners, got herself married with the complainant, by suppressing the fact that the petitioner no.1 was earlier married to Vikash Srivastava @ Vikash Kumar and the marriage of the petitioner no.1 with Vikash Srivastava @ Vikash Kumar was subsisting, on the date of marriage of the petitioner no.1 with the complainant.

4. The learned counsel for the petitioners relying upon the Judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Musstt Rehana Begum Vs. State of Assam & Another, reported in (2022) 3 S.C.R.
962 submits that in the facts of that case when the allegation against the accused of that case was that, the accused lady of that case was guilty of the offence punishable under Section 494 of the Indian Penal Code, because she was having a prior subsisting marriage, at the time of her marriage with the complainant of the case, the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India observed that allowing criminal proceeding to proceed for ( 2025:JHHC:15676 ) an offence punishable under Section 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code would constitute an abuse of the process, as the disputed fact as to whether there was a subsisting marriage on the date on which the accused of that case entered into marriage with the complainant of that case, is a subject matter of the conclusive finding, of the Family Court.

entities.text: Musstt Rehana Begum Vs. State of Assam & Another, reported in (2022) 3 S.C.R.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is next submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner that there is no allegation of entrustment of any property etc. upon any of the petitioners, hence, even if the entire allegation made against the petitioners are considered to be true in their entirety, still the offence punishable under Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code is not made out.

It is then submitted that there is no allegation of any deception played by the petitioners, to deliver any property, to any person and in the absence of the same, the offence punishable under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code is also not made out, even if the entire allegations made against the petitioners are considered to be true.
Hence, it is submitted that the prayer as prayed for by the petitioners in this criminal miscellaneous petition be allowed.

5. Learned Spl. P.P. and the learned counsel for the opposite party no.2 on the other hand vehemently opposes the prayer as prayed for by the petitioners in this criminal miscellaneous petition and submits that the petitioners have cheated the complainant by suppressing the material fact that the petitioner no.1 was having a prior subsisting marriage with Vikash ( 2025:JHHC:15676 ) Srivastava @ Vikash Kumar.
Hence, it is submitted that the entire criminal proceeding ought not to be quashed at this nascent stage.

6. Having heard the submissions made at the Bar and after going through the materials available in the record, it is pertinent to mention here that so far as the offence punishable under Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code is concerned, the essential ingredients to constitute the said offence are:-

(iii) There must be misappropriation or conversion to one's own use or use in violation of a legal direction of any legal contract, as has been reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Ram Narayan vs. Central Bureau of Investigation reported in (2003) 3 SCC 641.
7.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Now coming to the facts of the case, there is absolutely no allegation of any entrustment nor there is any allegation of dishonest misappropriation or conversion to one's own use or use in violation of any legal direction or of any legal contract.

In the absence of this essential ingredient, this Court has no hesitation in holding that even if the entire allegations made against the petitioners are considered to be true in their entirety, still the offence punishable under Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code is not made out.
( 2025:JHHC:15676 )
8.
So far as the offence punishable under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code is concerned, the essential ingredients to constitute the said offence are:-

(i) Deception of a person either by making a false or misleading representation or by dishonest concealment or by any other act or omission,
(ii) Fraudulent or dishonest inducement of that person to either deliver any property or to consent to the retention thereof by any person or to intentionally induce that person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived; and (iii) Such act or omission causing or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, as has been reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Mohammed Ibrahim & Ors. vs. State of Bihar & Anr,
reported in (2009) 8 SCC 751.
9.

In the absence of this essential ingredient to constitute the offence punishable under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, this Court has no hesitation in holding that even if the entire (
2025:JHHC:15676 ) allegations made against the petitioner are considered to be true in their entirety, still the offence punishable under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code is not made out.
10.

Since, neither the offence punishable under Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code nor the offence punishable under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code is made out against the petitioners, even if the entire allegations against the petitioners are considered to true in their entirety, this Court has no hesitation in holding that the continuation of this criminal proceeding against the petitioners will amount to abuse of process of the Court.
